title: The robber and the name
hookLine: a robber who can't say the name Rama is told to say it backwards, until an anthill grows over him
carry: the name, kept long and with love

cards: On day seven you met a robber on a forest road who asked his family to share the weight of his deeds, and they wouldn't. Here's a part of his story that day left out. He comes back to the sage shaken: what do I do now?
The sage gives him a word to repeat. Rama. And he can't say it.
A life of violence, the telling goes, has left the holy name stuck in his throat. So the sage turns it around. Say mara, then.
Mara, mara, mara. He sits down and says it, and the backwards word runs together: mara-mara-mara, rama-rama, Rama.

teach.b: He sits so long that an anthill grows over him. When he finally rises, the story says, he is Valmiki, named for valmika, the anthill, and he will sing the Ramayana.
This telling is later than the Ramayana itself, and versions differ on the sage. But many Hindus tell it to say something they believe deeply: the name of God works even when it's said badly.
What matters is that it's kept.

teach.h: NAMA JAPA: A NAME OF GOD, REPEATED.
teach.b: This is nama japa, repeating a name of God, Rama, Krishna, Shiva, and for many Hindus it is the heart of daily practice. Patanjali puts the same thing in two short lines.

teach.h: A LONG TIME. NO BREAK. WITH CARE.
teach.b: Practice becomes firmly rooted, sutra one fourteen says in paraphrase, when it is kept up for a long time, without a break, and with care. The word for care is satkara, which carries honor and devotion.

teach.h: OM: REPEAT IT, DWELL ON ITS MEANING.
teach.b: A little later he names the word itself: the word that expresses Ishvara, the Lord, is the syllable Om, and its japa goes with dwelling on its meaning. Repeat it, and turn toward what it points to.
Notice what neither the story nor the sutra counts. Not perfect pronunciation. Not a number of days; forty is a shape teachers and families give a sadhana.
Customs differ on what a lost day means for a vow, so ask the teacher or the elder whose practice it is.

teach.h: THE NAME, KEPT LONG, WITH LOVE.
teach.b: What both hold onto is the long arc and the love. A robber who could only say the name backwards became the poet of God.

how: Many Hindus keep nama japa, repeating a name of God such as Rama, Krishna or Shiva, often on a mala; those who take on a mantra sadhana may keep it at the same time each day, and customs differ on what happens if a day is lost.

o: the name of God, kept long and with care
a mantra that only works if it's pronounced perfectly
a mantra said once a year, on a festival day

games.q: the robber and the name — tap the pairs.
p: the backwards name the robber could say
an anthill, the root of Valmiki's name
the syllable Om, the word for the Lord

s: a name of God only works if you say it perfectly
in the well-loved telling, the robber could only say Rama backwards, and the name still changed him.
Patanjali pairs repeating Om with dwelling on its meaning
in sutras 1.27–28 the pranava is repeated and its meaning is turned over in the mind.
the Yoga Sutras set forty days as the length of a mantra practice
the sutra on practice names no number of days; it asks for a long time, no break, and care.

games.q: you're the sage. the robber wants to change, but he can't get the word Rama out. what do you do?
o: send him away until he can say it right.
give him mara to repeat, and let the name come round.
tell him a holy name isn't for someone like him.
games.why: in the telling, the sage turns the name around. repeated long enough, mara becomes Rama, and the robber rises as Valmiki.

practice: Take the mantra you've been keeping, or a name of God you love, or the syllable Om, and repeat it slowly. Don't worry about saying it perfectly.
Between repetitions, let a moment go to what it points toward: if you pray, that pointing can be your prayer, and if you don't, simply rest in the pause after the sound.

wordCard.voice: Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline, which, from Valmiki's anthill to Patanjali's sutra, grows firm through a long time and care.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: nama, name. Nama japa is repeating a name of God.

carryVoice: Your line: the name, kept long and with love. Even said backwards, it carried a robber home. Tomorrow, a sleep with its own name. See you then.

sources.ref: Valmiki the robber, the 'mara' japa and the anthill: a traditional telling, later than the Ramayana (one version in the Adhyatma Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda)
